models.summary: A light-use estimate of net primary productivity, then an age correction. Productivity is absorbed photosynthetically active radiation times a light-use efficiency. Daily radiation is clear-sky radiation times 0.248 plus 0.725 times a sunshine term. The printed term is the clear-sky sunshine itself, while the next sentence defines the sunshine percentage as the ratio of the two sunshine measures. Half of that daily total is taken as the photosynthetically active part, and the absorbed part is that half times the fraction the canopy takes. Efficiency is two temperature factors times a moisture factor times 0.389. Gross production is productivity plus respiration. Age is split into young under 41, middle-aged to 80, near mature to 100, mature to 140, and overripe past 141. Spruce productivity runs 10.56, 10.03, 8.81, 7.90, 7.21, with a printed average of 8.40 that is not the mean of those five. Scots pine runs 7.24, 7.38, 6.77, 6.77, 5.40, average 6.74. After maturity the rate falls, while the carbon already stored keeps rising. Products are log, plywood, and paper. A table prints 13.83, 54.97, and 31.20 under a lifespan heading, and those three sum to 100, so they are the shares. The year row prints 35 and 2, with 25 sitting off its cell.

models.summary: Three carbon pools and a harvest rule. The living pool is the productivity integrated over the stand that has not been cut. The product pool sums, over log, plywood, and paper, the share of the cut times the carbon still inside each product during its life. The dead pool is half of last year plus the newly dead. Total carbon is the sum of the three. Only mature and overmature trees are cut, older first. The rotation T and the cut ratio eta are chosen by simulation. Every tree cut or dead is replaced by a seedling, so the area stays constant. The loop ages the stand for 300 years and cuts when the year divides the rotation. On ten thousand square meters of Changbai, whose eight yearly productivities are averaged to 748 grams of carbon per square meter, the largest 100-year store is a 10-year rotation at a 20 percent cut: 3.57 times 10 to the 10 grams, against 3.09 with no cut. The eight yearly values average to 747.5, and the paper uses 748.

models.section: Forest Value by AHP and TOPSIS
models.summary: A three-criterion score of the same plans. Ecology is the 100-year carbon. Economy ignores product income, so carbon is not counted twice, and replaces planting and cutting cost by the area treated, entering the score as a cost. Tourism is a table. A zero cut scores 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, and 0.50 at 5, 10, 15, and 20 years. A full cut scores 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, and 0.25. The drop per extra cut grows with the wait, so it is not one constant step. The pairwise matrix is built from Google Scholar hit counts, 50.2, 19.1, and 12.2 million, and prints as rows 1, 3, 5; 1/3, 1, 1/8; 1/5, 8, 1. MATLAB is said to return a largest eigenvalue of 3.0 and weights 0.74, 0.18, and 0.08, with a consistency ratio of 0.038. An eigenvalue of 3.0 would make the consistency index zero, so the ratio 0.038 cannot belong to that eigenvalue. TOPSIS treats ecology and tourism as goods and economy as a cost. The highest score is 15 years and 40 percent. No plan is forbidden from cutting, and the no-cut plan scores lowest. An ornamental forest, Muchuan, prefers the long light cut, and an economic forest, Jhumpa, the short heavy cut.
